questions.:question/problem:
Simplify $2\cos(x-60^\circ)-\cos(x+60^\circ)$ using $\sin x$ and $\cos x$.

Enter signed coefficients:

{{field-1}} $\sin x+$ {{field-2}} $\cos x$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Use both cosine formulas:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\cos(u-v)&=\cos u\cos v+\sin u\sin v,\\
\cos(u+v)&=\cos u\cos v-\sin u\sin v.
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\cos 60^\circ=\frac{1}{2}$ and $\sin 60^\circ=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, the two expansions are

$$
\begin{aligned}
\cos(x-60^\circ)&=\frac{1}{2}\cos x+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\sin x,\\
\cos(x+60^\circ)&=\frac{1}{2}\cos x-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\sin x.
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $E=2\cos(x-60^\circ)-\cos(x+60^\circ)$. Substitute both expansions and distribute the factor $2$ and the subtraction:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E&=2\left(\frac{1}{2}\cos x+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\sin x\right)\\
&\quad-\left(\frac{1}{2}\cos x-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\sin x\right)\\
&=\cos x+\sqrt{3}\sin x\\
&\quad-\frac{1}{2}\cos x+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\sin x.
\end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the second expansion changes its negative sine term to a positive term. Collect like terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E&=\left(1-\frac{1}{2}\right)\cos x\\
&\quad+\left(\sqrt{3}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\sin x\\
&=\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\sin x+\frac{1}{2}\cos x.
\end{aligned}
$$

The coefficients are $\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and $\frac{1}{2}$, respectively.

questions.:question/problem: Express $\cos(x+180^\circ)$ in terms of $\sin x$ or $\cos x$.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Recall the sum formula for cosine:

$$
\cos(u+v)=\cos u\cos v-\sin u\sin v.
$$

Apply it with $u=x$ and $v=180^\circ$. Since $\cos 180^\circ=-1$ and $\sin 180^\circ=0$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\cos(x+180^\circ)&=\cos x\cos 180^\circ-\sin x\sin 180^\circ\\
&=\cos x\cdot(-1)-\sin x\cdot0\\
&=-\cos x.
\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the difference formula for cosine with $u = x$ and $v = 60^\circ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-{60}^{∘}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡{60}^{∘}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡{60}^{∘} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot \frac{1}{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{2} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
